summary:
Niger is an independent country with its own criminal law; the assessment below is national.

Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalises all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex and asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 100 million CFA francs, and the punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Same-sex sexual relations carry the same 5 to 10 year term and fine, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of a romantic relationship with a person of the same sex.

Creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 500 million CFA francs. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties.

Since March 2025, Article 24 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Since June 2026, marrying a person of the same sex and officiating, organising or bearing official witness to a same-sex wedding is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; Law 2015-36, which had prohibited discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged.

Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalised in 2026. Before that change the age of consent stood at 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts.

After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP.

Documented enforcement includes two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined; two young women in Maradi in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act; and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. As of 8-9 December 2022 Niger had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, and Maradi lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna had presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise same-sex relationships, with punishment unspecified and no debate scheduled.

No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness on those grounds were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organisations operated in secret, partly because they were not formally registered.

Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition, hindering relocation, and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers.

Gay men and lesbians face strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The only official cultural-values statement in the record concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values". The record contains no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.
tangentialFactors:
Niger's hybrid legal system layers a Sharia criminal track over the ordinary Penal Code. Human Rights Watch's 2004 survey listed twelve northern Nigerian states having adopted Sharia criminal provisions: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, a wave traced from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force from 27 January 2000. The provisions remain in force.

Niger State's own instrument, the Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000), was signed into law on 22 February 2000, came into operation on 4 May 2000 and was gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000. It amends the Penal Code Law Cap 94 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68, while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies.

The UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) sets out Nigeria's hybrid legal system, the twelve-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women, and the limits of the available arrest data.

Male prostitution was prevalent in Niamey, and effeminate men were known for having always been part of Niger's culture by organising traditional wedding ceremonies and supporting themselves that way. Niger's attitude toward LGBTQ issues is described as usually discreet.

outOfScopeNotes:
The record does not document any trans-specific killing or patterned violence against transgender people in Niger; the absence of reported violence may reflect underreporting driven by stigma or intimidation rather than its absence, and this remains unresolved.

Whether the February 2026 penal code's provisions on changing or attempting to change one's birth sex have been applied in any specific prosecution is not sourced here.

The record does not state whether Niger's criminal provisions apply to conduct occurring outside the country or to foreign nationals specifically beyond the general framework.

Enforcement data limits are acknowledged in the UK Home Office note; the actual scale of arrests under the 2026 code beyond the reported 'dozens' is unresolved.
